analysis.one_liner: Requires every employer to give workers a pension as good as federal employees get.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced; it has 12 Democratic supporters, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action since.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require every employer in America to either offer a retirement plan the Labor Secretary determines is as good as the Federal Employees Retirement System, or enroll its workers directly in FERS, the pension system federal employees use. FERS combines a guaranteed lifetime pension, Social Security, and a savings account with employer matching. Self-employed people would get the same choice. Small employers pay only part of the cost, with the federal Treasury covering the difference so workers still get the full benefit, and employers are barred from cutting pay because of the mandate.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers that currently offer nothing or only a modest 401(k), plus self-employed people who have no retirement plan at all. Millions of private-sector workers have no workplace retirement plan; this bill would give each of them a federal-style pension with guaranteed lifetime payments and employer contributions, not just a voluntary savings account.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without pensions and the self-employed

how_it_helps.text: Every employer must make available a retirement program the Secretary of Labor determines provides benefits comparable to FERS, or notify the Secretary that its employees will participate in FERS directly.
Self-employed individuals get the same choice: enroll in a comparable program or join FERS themselves.

Employers with annual revenue of $25 million or less pay only 50 percent of the required contributions, and the Secretary of the Treasury must credit the Thrift Savings Fund for the amount of the reduction, so the worker still receives the full benefit.
Small employers and self-employed people below the income thresholds get a new tax credit equal to 50 percent of their pension contributions, phasing down as revenue or income rises.
Employers may not reduce any form of employee compensation because of the new retirement requirement.

FERS is the retirement system for federal employees under chapter 84 of title 5, U.S. Code; in practice it combines a guaranteed pension based on years of service, Social Security, and a savings plan with employer matching contributions.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that do not already offer a FERS-comparable plan would take on a large new payroll cost — federal agencies pay most of the cost of the FERS pension plus matching savings contributions. The Treasury also absorbs the small-employer discount out of general tax revenue, and employers face a penalty of $10 per employee per day for noncompliance, capped at $500,000 a year for unintentional failures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers without pensions; taxpayers backfill small firms

drawbacks.text: The mandate is expensive: an employer without a comparable plan must begin paying the employer share of a full federal-style pension plus matching savings contributions, a cost that did not exist before, which could strain margins at low-margin businesses.
Employers that fail to comply owe $10 per employee per day, with a $500,000 annual cap for failures due to reasonable cause, and joint liability across commonly owned employers.
Whether an existing 401(k) or pension plan counts as 'comparable' to FERS is left to a Labor Secretary determination, creating uncertainty for employers who already offer generous plans.
The discount for small employers is backfilled by the Treasury, meaning general taxpayers pick up part of the cost of coverage at small firms rather than the employer.

Critics of broad employer mandates argue that new payroll costs of this size tend to come back out of wages or hiring; the bill's answer is an outright prohibition on cutting any form of compensation because of the requirement, but enforcement of that ban against subtle pay decisions would be difficult.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is real and large: guaranteed pension coverage for the many private-sector workers who have none. The cost side is also real and large: a new payroll obligation on employers and a federal backfill for small firms, at a scale that has made comparable employer mandates politically heavy lifts. The bill tries to soften the cost with small-employer discounts, tax credits, and a pay-cut ban, but it does not eliminate the underlying expense. An honest supporter would acknowledge this is one of the most expensive employer mandates ever drafted, and that its fate depends almost entirely on whether anyone is willing to vote for that cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to three House committees on the same day in February 2026, and none of them has taken it up yet; nothing has been scheduled, debated, or voted on.

narrative.text: Rep. Delia Ramirez introduced the Pensions for All Act in the House on February 12, 2026, with nine other original cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, and additionally to Oversight and Government Reform and Education and Workforce, for consideration of provisions within each committee's jurisdiction.
The bill has 11 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no action has been recorded since the referrals.
The 119th Congress remains in session through January 3, 2027, so the bill has not expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Because no committee has acted, employers' current retirement arrangements and costs are unchanged, and workers without pensions still have none. The bill's fate rests entirely on whether any of the three committees — most importantly Ways and Means, which handles the tax and contribution machinery — ever schedules it for consideration.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Undecided; employers' current costs unchanged for now

for.name: Rep. Delia Ramirez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the other original cosponsors on February 12, 2026.

for.name: Eleven House Democrats, including Reps. Tlaib, Carson, Thanedar, Garcia of Illinois, McIver, Lee of Pennsylvania, Stansbury, Omar, and McGovern
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no other members of either party have joined.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 supporters are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; no committee chair has scheduled the bill for action and no member has yet opposed it on the record.

industries.industry: Employers that do not offer pension plans
industries.note: They would have to start paying the employer share of a federal-style pension plus matching savings contributions — a cost their workers currently bear through having no retirement security. The industry's cost here is the workers' gain.

Employers could shift workers into FERS instead of private plans, moving assets out of the industry, but employers that keep private plans must make them FERS-comparable and could still be administered by these firms. Firms administering recordkeeping for the new comparable programs could keep or grow business.

They face new obligations but on discounted terms: half the normal contribution rate with the Treasury covering the gap, plus a 50 percent tax credit on contributions. Their interest in affordable terms runs alongside workers' interest in getting covered.

analysis.trajectory: With a dozen sponsors, all from one party, no Republican cosponsor, and a simultaneous referral to three committees, this bill faces the usual path of large employer-mandate proposals: it is likely to sit without a markup or a vote unless retirement policy unexpectedly becomes a priority. Committee chairs have taken no action in the weeks since introduction.
